CFDocument.title: Open Misconception Library
CFDocument.description: A public catalogue of misconceptions with stable IDs. One CFItem per misconception; humanCodingScheme carries the oml: identifier.
subject: Mathematics
Programming
CFDocument.notes: Generated from records/ by oml export case. 58 records.

CFItems.fullStatement: Mathematics
Programming
A decimal with more digits after the point is a larger number, because the digits after the point make a bigger whole number.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Longer decimal is larger
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'compare two decimals where the shorter is larger', chooses the decimal with more digits after the point. Example: Which is larger, 0.5 or 0.25? -> 0.25 (expected 0.5).

CFItems.fullStatement: A decimal with fewer digits after the point is a larger number, because more digits mean smaller pieces, like a fraction with a bigger denominator.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Shorter decimal is larger
CFItems.notes: kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'compare two decimals where the longer decimal is larger', chooses the decimal with fewer digits after the point. Example: Which is larger, 0.85 or 0.8? -> 0.8 (expected 0.85).

CFItems.fullStatement: Fractions are added by adding the numerators together and adding the denominators together, treating the top and bottom numbers as independent whole numbers, the same way fractions are multiplied.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Adding fractions across numerators and denominators
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: reviewed. Evidence: on 'add two fractions with unlike denominators', response numerator = a + c and response denominator = b + d for a/b + c/d, with no attempt at a common denominator. Example: 1/2 + 1/3 -> 2/5 (expected 5/6).

CFItems.fullStatement: To add fractions you add the numerators and keep the denominator, whichever denominator is written, because the denominator is just a label that does not take part in the sum.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Adding numerators and keeping one denominator
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'add two fractions with unlike denominators', response numerator = a + c; response denominator is one of the given denominators (usually the first or the larger), with no conversion of the addends. Example: 1/2 + 1/3 -> 2/3 (expected 5/6).

CFItems.fullStatement: To add a whole number and a fraction you add the whole number to the numerator.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Adding a whole number to the numerator
CFItems.notes: kind: procedural-bug. status: draft. Evidence: on 'add a whole number and a proper fraction', adds the whole number to the numerator and keeps the denominator. Example: 2 + 1/3 = ? -> 3/3 (= 1) (expected 2 1/3 (= 7/3)).

CFItems.fullStatement: The fraction with the bigger denominator is the bigger fraction, because the denominator is a bigger number.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Bigger denominator means bigger fraction
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'compare two unit fractions', picks the unit fraction with the larger denominator as larger; on 1/b vs 1/d chooses the one with the larger b. Example: Which is larger, 1/3 or 1/8? -> 1/8 (expected 1/3).

CFItems.fullStatement: A fraction is simplified by crossing out a digit that appears in both the numerator and the denominator.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Cancelling matching digits
CFItems.notes: kind: notation-confusion. status: draft. Evidence: on 'simplify a fraction whose numerator and denominator share a digit', deletes the shared digit from both numbers. Example: Simplify 12/24 -> 1/4 (cancelling the 2s) (expected 1/2).

CFItems.fullStatement: The size of a fraction is decided by how many pieces are missing from the whole; fractions with the same gap between numerator and denominator are equal.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Comparing fractions by the gap between numerator and denominator
CFItems.notes: kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'compare two fractions with the same numerator-denominator gap', declares the fractions equal because each is the same number of pieces short of one whole. Example: Which is larger, 5/6 or 7/8? -> They are the same (expected 7/8).

CFItems.fullStatement: To compare two fractions you compare the numerators and the denominators as whole numbers; a fraction with bigger numbers is a bigger fraction.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Comparing fractions by their whole-number parts
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'compare two fractions where the larger fraction has the smaller numerator and denominator', chooses the fraction whose numerator and denominator are both larger. Example: Which is larger, 4/5 or 5/9? -> 5/9 (expected 4/5).

CFItems.fullStatement: To multiply two fractions you multiply diagonally: the first numerator by the second denominator over the first denominator by the second numerator.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Cross-multiplying to multiply fractions
CFItems.notes: kind: procedural-bug. status: draft. Evidence: on 'multiply two proper fractions', product numerator = a x d and product denominator = b x c for a/b x c/d. Example: 2/3 x 4/5 = ? -> 10/12 (expected 8/15).

CFItems.fullStatement: In a division the bigger number must be divided by the smaller number, so if the divisor is bigger the two numbers should be swapped.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: You can only divide a larger number by a smaller one
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'divide a fraction by a larger whole number', swaps dividend and divisor so that the larger number is divided by the smaller. Example: 1/2 / 3 = ? -> 6 (expected 1/6).

CFItems.fullStatement: Dividing always gives a result smaller than the number you started with, so dividing by a fraction cannot make a number bigger.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Division always makes smaller
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'predict whether a quotient will be larger or smaller than the dividend, without calculating', predicts the quotient of a number divided by a proper fraction is smaller than the number. Example: Without calculating, is 6 / 1/2 more or less than 6? -> Less (expected More (it is 12)).

CFItems.fullStatement: Dividing means sharing a quantity equally among a number of people, so a division by a fraction has no meaning and must be a mistake or a different operation.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Division of fractions only means sharing
CFItems.notes: kind: undergeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'choose the operation for a measurement-division word problem', rejects division and multiplies or divides by the wrong number, because 'you can't share among half a person'. Example: How many 1/2-cup servings are in 3 cups? -> 3 / 2 = 1.5 (or 3 x 2 = 6 'because it can't be division') (expected 3 / 1/2 = 6).

CFItems.fullStatement: You get an equivalent fraction by adding the same number to the numerator and the denominator, or by subtracting the same number from both.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Equivalent fractions by adding the same number
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'complete an equivalent fraction with a given denominator', adds the difference in denominators to the numerator. Example: 2/3 = ?/6 -> 5/6 (expected 4/6).

CFItems.fullStatement: A fraction is written as a decimal by putting its numerator, or its denominator, after the decimal point.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Writing a fraction as a decimal by copying its digits
CFItems.notes: kind: notation-confusion. status: draft. Evidence: on 'convert a unit fraction to a decimal', writes 0.<denominator>. Example: Write 1/4 as a decimal -> 0.4 (expected 0.25).

CFItems.fullStatement: A fraction is always part of one whole, so the numerator can never be bigger than the denominator and a fraction can never be greater than 1.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: A fraction cannot be more than one whole
CFItems.notes: kind: undergeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'add two proper fractions whose sum exceeds one', adjusts the result so it stays below or equal to one. Example: 3/4 + 3/4 = ? -> 6/8 (or 1) (expected 6/4 (= 1 1/2)).

CFItems.fullStatement: To divide fractions you flip both fractions and then multiply.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Inverting both fractions when dividing
CFItems.notes: kind: procedural-bug. status: draft. Evidence: on 'divide two proper fractions', inverts both dividend and divisor and multiplies. Example: 1/2 / 3/4 = ? -> 8/3 (expected 2/3).

CFItems.fullStatement: To divide fractions you flip the first fraction and then multiply.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Inverting the first fraction when dividing
CFItems.notes: kind: procedural-bug. status: draft. Evidence: on 'divide two proper fractions', inverts the dividend instead of the divisor and multiplies. Example: 1/2 / 3/4 = ? -> 6/4 (= 3/2) (expected 2/3).

CFItems.fullStatement: To write a mixed number as an improper fraction you add the whole number to the numerator and keep the denominator.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Converting a mixed number by adding all its numbers
CFItems.notes: kind: procedural-bug. status: draft. Evidence: on 'convert a mixed number to an improper fraction', numerator = whole + numerator; denominator unchanged. Example: Write 2 1/3 as an improper fraction -> 3/3 (expected 7/3).

CFItems.fullStatement: Multiplying always gives a result larger than the number you started with, so multiplying by a fraction cannot make a number smaller.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Multiplication always makes bigger
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'predict whether a product will be larger or smaller than a factor, without calculating', predicts the product of a number and a proper fraction is larger than the number. Example: Without calculating, is 8 x 3/4 more or less than 8? -> More (expected Less).

CFItems.fullStatement: To multiply mixed numbers you multiply the whole numbers together and the fractions together and put the two results back together.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Multiplying mixed numbers part by part
CFItems.notes: kind: procedural-bug. status: draft. Evidence: on 'multiply two mixed numbers', product = (whole x whole) and (fraction x fraction) written as a mixed number; the cross terms are dropped. Example: 2 1/2 x 3 1/3 = ? -> 6 1/6 (expected 8 1/3).

CFItems.fullStatement: Before multiplying fractions you must write them with a common denominator, then multiply the numerators and keep the denominator.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Multiplying needs a common denominator
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'multiply two fractions with unlike denominators', converts to a common denominator, multiplies numerators and keeps the common denominator. Example: 1/2 x 1/3 = ? -> 3/6 x 2/6 = 6/6 = 1 (expected 1/6).

CFItems.fullStatement: Fractions come one after another like whole numbers, so between two fractions that are 'next to each other' there is no other number.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: No number between neighbouring fractions
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'ask how many numbers lie between two fractions', answers none, or a small finite count found by listing. Example: How many numbers are there between 1/5 and 2/5? -> None (expected Infinitely many).

CFItems.fullStatement: On a number line the fraction refers to the whole line drawn, so 1/2 is at the middle of the line wherever the line ends.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: The whole line is the whole
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'place a fraction on a number line longer than one unit', places the fraction at that fraction of the whole drawn segment rather than of the unit interval. Example: Mark 1/2 on a number line from 0 to 3 -> at 1 1/2, the middle of the line (expected halfway between 0 and 1).

CFItems.fullStatement: To find a/b of a quantity you divide the quantity by a and multiply by b.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Swapping numerator and denominator when finding a fraction of a quantity
CFItems.notes: kind: procedural-bug. status: draft. Evidence: on 'find a non-unit fraction of a whole-number quantity', divides by the numerator and multiplies by the denominator. Example: Find 3/4 of 20 -> 26 2/3 (20 / 3 x 4) (expected 15).

CFItems.fullStatement: A fraction compares the shaded part with the unshaded part, so the number of shaded pieces goes on top and the number of unshaded pieces goes underneath.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Writing the shaded part over the unshaded part
CFItems.notes: kind: notation-confusion. status: draft. Evidence: on 'name the fraction shaded in a shape divided into equal parts', writes shaded/unshaded instead of shaded/total. Example: A bar is cut into 5 equal parts and 3 are shaded. What fraction is shaded? -> 3/2 (expected 3/5).

CFItems.fullStatement: Fractions are subtracted by subtracting the numerators and subtracting the denominators.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Subtracting fractions across numerators and denominators
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'subtract two fractions with unlike denominators', difference numerator = a - c and difference denominator = b - d for a/b - c/d. Example: 3/4 - 1/2 = ? -> 2/2 (= 1) (expected 1/4).

CFItems.fullStatement: A fraction is two whole numbers written one above the other, not a single number with its own size; the numerator and denominator can be read and handled separately.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: A fraction is two separate whole numbers
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'place a fraction on a number line marked 0 to 10', places the fraction at the numerator, the denominator, or their sum. Example: Mark 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 10 -> at 3 (or at 4, or at 7) (expected between 0 and 1, three quarters of the way).

CFItems.fullStatement: If a shape is cut into b pieces, each piece is one b-th of the shape, whether or not the pieces are the same size.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Any part of a shape cut into b pieces is 1/b
CFItems.notes: kind: missing-prerequisite. status: draft. Evidence: on 'name the fraction shaded in a shape divided into unequal parts', counts pieces and writes shaded/total, ignoring the sizes of the pieces. Example: A rectangle is cut into 4 pieces of different sizes; the largest is shaded. What fraction is shaded? -> 1/4 (expected Cannot tell from the count; it is more than 1/4).

CFItems.fullStatement: An array gets bigger by itself when you store something past its end, so its size does not need to be decided in advance.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Arrays grow when you add to them

CFItems.fullStatement: You get the length of an array by calling a method on it, in the same way as for a string or a list.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: An array's length is a method call
CFItems.notes: kind: notation-confusion. status: draft. Evidence: on 'write the length of an array', writes length() or size() on an array. Example: Given int[] a, write an expression for its length. -> a.length() (or a.size()) (expected a.length).

CFItems.fullStatement: A boolean variable or expression cannot be used directly as a condition; it has to be compared with true or false first, and a comparison is the only thing that produces a condition.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: A boolean must be compared with true to be used as a condition
CFItems.notes: kind: undergeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'write a condition from a boolean variable', writes == true (or == True) and cannot explain what if done: alone would do. Example: done is a boolean. Write the condition for 'if done'. -> if done == True: (expected if done:).

CFItems.fullStatement: A logical and or or always evaluates both of its operands, whatever the first one turns out to be.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Both operands of and/or are always evaluated

CFItems.fullStatement: In an if-else statement the if branch runs when the condition is true and then the else branch runs afterwards as well, because it comes next in the code.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Both branches of an if-else run in turn

CFItems.fullStatement: The body of an if statement keeps running for as long as the condition is true, like a while loop.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: An if statement repeats while its condition holds
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'trace an if statement whose body keeps its condition true', predicts repeated execution of the body. Example: x = 0
if x < 3:
    x = x + 1
print(x) -> 3 (expected 1).

CFItems.fullStatement: Every time a loop body starts again, the variables changed inside it go back to what they were before the loop.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Variables reset at the start of every loop iteration
CFItems.notes:
kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'trace an accumulator updated inside a loop', reports the value from a single iteration rather than the accumulated value. Example: total = 0
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    total = total + n
print(total) -> 3 (expected 6).

CFItems.fullStatement: The condition of a while loop is watched continuously, so the loop exits in the middle of the body the moment the condition turns false.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: A while loop stops the instant its condition becomes false
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'trace a while loop whose condition becomes false partway through the body', stops the trace before the rest of the body runs on the final iteration. Example: i = 0
while i < 2:
    i = i + 1
    print(i) -> 1 (expected 1
2).

CFItems.fullStatement: Every line of a program is active at the same time, so a later line can affect what an earlier line did, and a condition anywhere is watched continuously.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: All the statements in a program are active at once
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'trace a program where a later assignment would matter if it applied retroactively', applies the later value to the earlier output. Example: x = 1
print(x)
x = 2 -> 2 (expected 1).

CFItems.fullStatement: The computer understands the purpose of the program and fills in steps that were left out, so a program does what you meant as long as the intention is clear.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: The computer fills in what you meant
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'predict the output of a program with a missing step', predicts the intended output rather than the literal one. Example: numbers = [3, 1, 2]
print(numbers)  # print sorted -> [1, 2, 3] (expected [3, 1, 2]).

CFItems.fullStatement: The variable passed to a function has to have the same name as the parameter, or the function will not receive it.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Arguments are matched to parameters by name
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'predict the output of a call whose argument name differs from the parameter name', predicts an error or that the parameter is unset. Example: def show(n):
    print(n)
value = 5
show(value) -> Error: n is not defined (or 'nothing') (expected 5).

CFItems.fullStatement: A recursive function stops calling itself when there is nothing left to do, so it does not need an explicit base case.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: A recursive function stops by itself
CFItems.notes:
kind: missing-prerequisite. status: draft. Evidence: on 'predict the behaviour of a recursive function with no base case', predicts termination with a sensible answer. Example: def count_down(n):
    print(n)
    count_down(n - 1)
count_down(3) -> 3 2 1 (expected 3 2 1 0 -1 ... until the recursion limit is hit).

CFItems.fullStatement: return a, b sends back two separate values, so the caller receives two things rather than one tuple.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: A function can return several separate values
CFItems.notes:
kind: undergeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'predict the type of a call that returns a comma-separated list', predicts two values, or that the second is lost, rather than one tuple. Example: def f():
    return 1, 2
x = f()
print(type(x)) -> int (or 'error, two values into one variable') (expected <class 'tuple'>).

CFItems.fullStatement: A parameter is the same variable as the argument that was passed in, so assigning to the parameter inside the function changes the caller's variable, even for numbers and strings.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Changing a parameter changes the caller's variable
CFItems.notes:
kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'trace a function that reassigns a primitive parameter', reports the caller's variable as changed. Example: def bump(n):
    n = n + 1
x = 1
bump(x)
print(x) -> 2 (expected 1).

CFItems.fullStatement: A function gives its result back by printing it, so a function that prints its answer can be used in an expression, and return is just another way to display.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Printing a value is the same as returning it
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'use the result of a function that prints instead of returning', expects the printed value to be available to the caller. Example: def double(n):
    print(n * 2)
x = double(4)
print(x + 1) -> 9 (expected 8 then TypeError (x is None)).

CFItems.fullStatement: A recursive call is a jump back to the beginning of the function, using the same variables, so there is only ever one copy of the function running.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: A recursive call jumps back to the start
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'trace a recursive function that does work after the recursive call', omits or misorders the work done after each call returns. Example: def show(n):
    if n == 0:
        return
    show(n - 1)
    print(n)
show(3) -> 3 2 1 (or nothing, or 1 only) (expected 1
2
3).

CFItems.fullStatement: Assigning one object variable to another makes a second, independent copy of the object, so changing one does not affect the other.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Assigning an object makes a copy
CFItems.notes:
kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'trace a mutation through an aliased object', reports the other variable's object as unchanged. Example: a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a) -> [1, 2] (expected [1, 2, 3]).

CFItems.fullStatement: Declaring an object variable final or const makes the object it refers to unchangeable, so its fields or elements cannot be modified.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: A constant reference means an unchangeable object

CFItems.fullStatement: A constructor creates the object and has to return it at the end, so a constructor without a return statement produces nothing.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: A constructor must return the object
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'write a constructor', adds return this (or return self) at the end, or a return type to the constructor header. Example: Write a constructor for Point that stores x and y. -> Point Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; return this; } (expected Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }).

CFItems.fullStatement: Comparing two object variables with == compares what is inside the objects, so two objects with the same field values are equal.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: == compares the contents of objects

CFItems.fullStatement: An object variable contains the object itself, not a reference to it, so every variable is its own object and passing it around passes the object.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: A variable contains the whole object
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'draw or describe memory after two variables refer to one object', draws two separate objects, one inside each variable. Example: p = Point(1, 2)
q = p
Draw p and q. -> Two boxes, each containing a Point(1, 2) (expected Two variables, both pointing to one Point object).

CFItems.fullStatement: In an expression that mixes strings and numbers with +, the numbers are added together first and the string is attached afterwards.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Plus adds numbers before it concatenates
CFItems.notes: kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'predict a left-to-right mixed concatenation', adds the numeric operands regardless of their position. Example: System.out.println("x" + 1 + 2); -> x3 (expected x12).

CFItems.fullStatement: Dividing one whole number by another gives the exact mathematical result with a fractional part, whatever the types involved.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Dividing two integers gives a fraction
CFItems.notes:
kind: overgeneralization. status: draft. Evidence: on 'predict the result of integer division in a language that truncates', predicts the exact quotient. Example: int x = 7 / 2;
System.out.println(x); -> 3.5 (expected 3).

CFItems.fullStatement: The equals sign in an assignment states that the two sides are equal, as in algebra, so x = x + 1 is a contradiction and a = b and b = a mean the same thing.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Assignment states an equation
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'trace an assignment whose right-hand side uses the variable being assigned', declares the statement impossible or leaves the variable unchanged. Example: x = 5
x = x + 1
What is x? -> 'Impossible, x can't equal x + 1' (or 5) (expected 6).

CFItems.fullStatement: After a = b the two variables are connected, so whenever b changes later, a changes too.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Assignment links two variables
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'trace a change to the source variable after an assignment between primitives', reports the destination variable as having the source's new value. Example: a = 1
b = a
a = 7
What is b? -> 7 (expected 1).

CFItems.fullStatement: Assigning a = b moves the value from b into a, so b is empty or zero afterwards.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Assignment moves the value out of the source
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'trace the source variable after an assignment', reports the source as empty, zero or undefined. Example: b = 4
a = b
What is b? -> 0 (or 'nothing') (expected 4).

CFItems.fullStatement: The name of a variable tells the computer what it is for, so a variable called total will add things up and one called largest will hold the biggest value.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: The computer understands variable names
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'predict the value of a descriptively named variable that is never updated', predicts the value the name suggests rather than the value assigned. Example: largest = 0
for n in [4, 9, 2]:
    pass
print(largest) -> 9 (expected 0).

CFItems.fullStatement: A variable that has been declared but never assigned holds zero, or an empty value, so it can be safely read or added to.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Uninitialised variables start at zero

CFItems.fullStatement: A variable stores every value ever assigned to it, so an earlier value can still be read out later.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: A variable remembers every value it has held
CFItems.notes:
kind: misapplied-analogy. status: draft. Evidence: on 'trace repeated assignment to one variable and then use it', uses an earlier value, or sums the values, instead of the most recent one. Example: x = 3
x = 5
print(x) -> 3 5 (or 8) (expected 5).
